--- title: "Inter-rater reliability: Bree’s coding and the model coding" author: "Manuel Alcalá Kovalski, Urban Institute" date: today toc-depth: 2 execute: warning: false message: false --- The plan for the open-ended answers and the interview transcripts is that a language model applies Bree’s codebook to everything, and Bree codes a random sample by hand to check it. This page is the first of those checks. It compares Bree’s coding of the answers in her September sample with two model runs from October 6, one by Claude Sonnet 5 and one by Claude Opus 5.5. All data presented in this document are preliminary and not for publication or dissemination. Inter-rater reliability usually describes two trained people coding the same material. Here one of the two raters is a model and Bree is the reference, so the numbers say how closely each model reproduces her coding. How closely two people would agree is not measured yet; that needs a second person to code the same answers. ## What Bree coded Bree drew a random 15 percent of the data delivered by September 22, which came to one survey file, one canvassing file, and two interviews, and coded the survey and canvassing files in NVivo. Her coding log on Box marks the files she has finished and the codebook version she used: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} log <- read_excel(coding_log, sheet = "Details") |> filter(str_to_lower(`Coding complete`) == "yes") # a log cell can list several files separated by "/" coded_files <- log$`Raw file name` |> str_split("/") |> unlist() |> str_trim() |> discard(\(f) f == "") log |> transmute( File = `Raw file name` |> str_remove("[\\s/]+$"), Tool = `Data collection tool type`, `Codebook version` = `Codebook version used` ) |> tbl() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The two interviews in her sample are not coded yet, so this page covers open-ended answers only. ## Matching her coding to the answers NVivo exports each coded passage as its text, without the respondent’s ID. Each passage is matched to an answer in those files by its text, ignoring case, punctuation, and spacing. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # text as compared: lower case, no punctuation, single spaces match_key <- function(x) { x |> str_to_lower() |> str_remove_all("[^\\w\\s]") |> str_squish() } nvivo <- read_excel( nvivo_export, col_names = c("code", "path", "source", "text"), skip = 1, col_types = "text" ) # every code in Bree's NVivo project is listed, coded or not: that is her # codebook. NVivo names carry stray spaces ("NEED _OTHER") bree_codes <- nvivo |> filter(str_starts(path, "Codes")) |> distinct(code = str_remove_all(code, "\\s")) |> pull(code) not_in_v6 <- setdiff(bree_codes, codebook$code) if (length(not_in_v6) > 0) { cli::cli_abort("Codes in Bree's NVivo export that are not in codebook.csv: {not_in_v6}") } # a few selections run one cell past the answer and pick up the respondent's # Unique ID on its own line: drop ID-only and blank lines passages <- nvivo |> filter(!is.na(text)) |> mutate( code = str_remove_all(code, "\\s"), picked_up_id = str_detect(text, "\n\\s*\\d+\\s*(\n|$)"), text = text |> str_split("\n") |> map_chr(\(lines) str_c(lines[!str_detect(lines, "^\\s*\\d*\\s*$")], collapse = " ")), key = match_key(text) ) sampled <- answers |> filter(str_trim(str_remove(delivery, "\\.xlsx$")) %in% coded_files) |> mutate(key = match_key(text)) unmatched <- anti_join(passages, sampled, by = "key") if (nrow(unmatched) > 0) { cli::cli_abort("{nrow(unmatched)} coded passage{?s} match no answer in Bree's files") } # identical answers in the same file cannot be told apart by text. Bree coded # each copy, so a code applied to k identical answers appears k times duplicates <- count(sampled, key, name = "n_answers") |> filter(n_answers > 1) uneven <- passages |> count(key, code, name = "n_rows") |> inner_join(duplicates, by = "key") |> filter(n_rows != n_answers) if (nrow(uneven) > 0) { cli::cli_abort("A code covers only some copies of an answer that appears more than once") } bree <- passages |> inner_join(select(sampled, answer_id, key), by = "key", relationship = "many-to-many") |> distinct(answer_id, code) |> mutate(coder = "Bree") scope <- sampled |> semi_join(bree, by = "answer_id") |> select(answer_id, tool, question, text) ``` ::: The export has 120 rows, one for each code applied to a passage, and every row matched an answer (the code stops if one does not). In 12 rows Bree’s selection ran one cell past the answer and picked up the respondent’s Unique ID; that line is dropped before matching. 4 of the answers Bree coded share their text with another answer in her files. She coded every copy the same way, so each copy keeps those codes. Bree gave at least one code to all 71 answers in her files: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scope |> count(Question = question_label(question), name = "Answers") |> tbl() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Keeping the comparison like for like - **Same answers**: only the answers Bree coded are compared. - **Same list of codes**: Bree used codebook version 5 (145 codes) and the models used version 6, which adds 22 codes and renames none. The models’ uses of the new codes are set aside (table below), so every coder chooses from the same 145 codes. - **Same unit**: one answer. A code counts once per answer, however many passages of the answer it was applied to. - **Same domains**: every code is placed in its version 6 domain for all three coders. No code changed domain between versions. - **Still open: what gets coded.** The models are told to “assign every code whose definition the passage clearly meets,” including codes from different domains, such as who the person cares for or what has been hard. Whether Bree codes everything an answer mentions or only what responds to the question is a question for her. The domain table below shows how much of the difference this accounts for. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model_raw <- imap(runs, \(run, coder) { read_csv(here("data/processed/llm-coding", run, "coded_open_ended.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |> filter(answer_id %in% scope$answer_id) |> mutate(coder = coder) }) |> list_rbind() # every coded answer has at least one row in a run, even with no codes missing <- scope |> cross_join(tibble(coder = names(runs))) |> anti_join(model_raw, by = c("answer_id", "coder")) if (nrow(missing) > 0) { cli::cli_abort("{nrow(missing)} of Bree's answers are missing from a model run") } model_used <- model_raw |> filter(!is.na(code)) |> distinct(coder, answer_id, code) set_aside <- model_used |> filter(!code %in% bree_codes) coded <- model_used |> filter(code %in% bree_codes) |> bind_rows(bree) set_aside |> count(coder, code) |> pivot_wider(names_from = coder, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |> rename(`Version 6 code` = code) |> tbl( title = "Model codes set aside because they are not in version 5", note = "Number of answers each model gave the code." ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Model codes set aside because they are not in version 5

Number of answers each model gave the code.

``` ::: ::: ## How closely the coders agree Each table compares two coders on the 71 answers: - **Identical codes**: the share of answers where both chose exactly the same codes. - **Average overlap**: for each answer, the codes both chose divided by the codes either chose, averaged over answers. 1 means identical, 0 means nothing in common. - **First coder’s codes the second also chose** and the reverse: for Bree and a model, the first is the share of Bree’s codes the model found, the second the share of the model’s codes Bree also used. - **Krippendorff’s alpha**: agreement corrected for the agreement two coders would reach by chance, given how often each code is used. 1 is perfect agreement and 0 is no better than chance. When two coders choose different but overlapping sets of codes, the MASI distance gives partial credit ([Passonneau 2006](https://aclanthology.org/L06-1392/)). Krippendorff (2004, *Content Analysis*, 2nd ed.) recommends relying on coding with alpha of at least 0.80 and treating 0.67 to 0.80 as enough only for tentative conclusions. The brackets are 95 percent intervals from resampling the answers 2,000 times. With this few answers they are wide; differences between the two models that fall inside them are not meaningful. The second table repeats the comparison one level up: instead of the exact codes, which domains (Desired Supports, Challenges, and so on) each coder used on the answer. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # share of codes in common: both empty counts as identical jaccard <- function(a, b) { either <- union(a, b) if (length(either) == 0) return(1) length(intersect(a, b)) / length(either) } # MASI distance between two coders' code sets for one answer (Passonneau 2006): # 0 = identical sets, 1 = nothing in common, with partial credit in between. masi_distance <- function(a, b) { # TODO(Manu): return the distance between code sets `a` and `b` NA_real_ } # distance between every pair of code sets, filled once so the bootstrap only # indexes into it distance_matrix <- function(sets, distance) { n <- length(sets) d <- matrix(0, n, n) for (i in seq_len(n - 1)) { for (j in (i + 1):n) d[i, j] <- d[j, i] <- distance(sets[[i]], sets[[j]]) } d } # Krippendorff's alpha for two coders: 1 - observed / expected disagreement. # `d` holds the first coder's sets, then the second's, so answer i is row i # and row n + i. Observed: the two coders on the same answer. Expected: any # two sets drawn from all the sets both coders produced. alpha_from_distances <- function(d, idx) { n <- nrow(d) / 2 pooled <- c(idx, n + idx) observed <- mean(d[cbind(idx, n + idx)]) m <- length(pooled) expected <- sum(d[pooled, pooled]) / (m * (m - 1)) 1 - observed / expected } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # one code set per coder per answer, in scope order; no codes = empty set code_sets <- map(set_names(coders), \(who) { sets <- coded |> filter(coder == who) |> summarise(codes = list(sort(code)), .by = answer_id) left_join(select(scope, answer_id), sets, by = "answer_id") |> pull(codes) |> map(\(x) x %||% character()) }) domain_of <- set_names(codebook$domain, codebook$code) domain_sets <- map(code_sets, \(sets) map(sets, \(s) sort(unique(unname(domain_of[s]))))) pair_agreement <- function(x, y) { per_answer <- tibble( identical = map2_lgl(x, y, setequal), overlap = map2_dbl(x, y, jaccard), both = lengths(map2(x, y, intersect)), n_x = lengths(x), n_y = lengths(y) ) d <- distance_matrix(c(x, y), masi_distance) measures <- function(idx) { p <- per_answer[idx, ] c( "Identical codes" = mean(p$identical), "Average overlap" = mean(p$overlap), "First coder’s codes the second also chose" = sum(p$both) / sum(p$n_x), "Second coder’s codes the first also chose" = sum(p$both) / sum(p$n_y), "Krippendorff’s alpha (MASI)" = alpha_from_distances(d, idx) ) } estimate <- measures(seq_len(nrow(per_answer))) boot <- replicate(n_boot, measures(sample(nrow(per_answer), replace = TRUE))) tibble( measure = names(estimate), estimate, low = apply(boot, 1, quantile, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE), high = apply(boot, 1, quantile, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE) ) } pairs <- list(c("Bree", "Sonnet"), c("Bree", "Opus"), c("Sonnet", "Opus")) agreement_table <- function(sets) { map(pairs, \(p) pair_agreement(sets[[p[1]]], sets[[p[2]]]) |> mutate(pair = str_c(p[1], " and ", p[2]))) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(shown = case_when( is.na(estimate) ~ "not yet computed", str_detect(measure, "alpha|overlap") ~ sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", estimate, low, high), .default = sprintf("%.0f%% (%.0f–%.0f)", 100 * estimate, 100 * low, 100 * high) )) |> select(Measure = measure, pair, shown) |> pivot_wider(names_from = pair, values_from = shown) } agreement_table(code_sets) |> tbl(title = "Agreement on the exact codes") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Agreement on the exact codes

``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} agreement_table(domain_sets) |> tbl(title = "Agreement on the domains") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Agreement on the domains

``` ::: ::: ## How many codes each coder uses, and where ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} map(coders, \(who) tibble( Coder = who, `Codes per answer` = round(mean(lengths(code_sets[[who]])), 1), `Answers with no code` = sum(lengths(code_sets[[who]]) == 0) )) |> list_rbind() |> tbl() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Answers on which each coder used at least one code from each domain. A domain the models use often and Bree rarely points to a difference in what gets coded, not in how a code is read. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coded |> mutate(domain = domain_of[code]) |> distinct(coder, answer_id, domain) |> count(domain, coder) |> pivot_wider(names_from = coder, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |> select(Domain = domain, all_of(coders)) |> arrange(desc(Bree), desc(Sonnet)) |> tbl(note = str_glue("Number of answers, out of {nrow(scope)}.")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Number of answers, out of 71.

``` ::: ::: ## Agreement code by code Each code Bree used on at least five answers: how many answers each coder gave it, how many both did, and Cohen’s kappa for that code (1 is perfect agreement, 0 is no better than chance). With this few answers per code, these are a guide to where to look, not estimates to report. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cohen_kappa <- function(x, y) { observed <- mean(x == y) expected <- mean(x) * mean(y) + mean(!x) * mean(!y) (observed - expected) / (1 - expected) } frequent <- bree |> count(code) |> filter(n >= 5) |> pull(code) map(frequent, \(cd) { has <- map(code_sets, \(sets) map_lgl(sets, \(s) cd %in% s)) tibble( Code = cd, Bree = sum(has$Bree), Sonnet = sum(has$Sonnet), `Both (Sonnet)` = sum(has$Bree & has$Sonnet), `Kappa (Sonnet)` = round(cohen_kappa(has$Bree, has$Sonnet), 2), Opus = sum(has$Opus), `Both (Opus)` = sum(has$Bree & has$Opus), `Kappa (Opus)` = round(cohen_kappa(has$Bree, has$Opus), 2) ) }) |> list_rbind() |> arrange(desc(Bree)) |> tbl() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Codes most often swapped When Bree and a model disagree on an answer, which of Bree’s codes the model left out and which code it chose instead. Pairs that recur point to codes whose boundary the codebook could draw more sharply. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} swaps <- map(names(runs), \(model) { map2(code_sets$Bree, code_sets[[model]], \(b, m) { expand_grid(`Bree chose` = setdiff(b, m), `Model chose instead` = setdiff(m, b)) }) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(coder = model) }) |> list_rbind() swaps |> count(`Bree chose`, `Model chose instead`, coder) |> pivot_wider(names_from = coder, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |> mutate(total = Sonnet + Opus) |> filter(total >= 4) |> arrange(desc(total)) |> select(-total) |> tbl(note = "Number of answers. Pairs seen on fewer than four answers across both models are not shown.") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Number of answers. Pairs seen on fewer than four answers across both models are not shown.

``` ::: ::: ## What this shows so far - **Where Bree and the models code the same thing, they mostly agree.** On child care, senior care, affordability, and care for everyone, kappa is above 0.6 for both models. - **Two of Bree’s codes account for about half of what the models miss.** Of the 58 codes Bree chose that Sonnet did not, 28 are `NEED_HIGH_QUALITY_CARE` or `NEED_OTHER` (Opus: 29 of 62). Bree uses `NEED_HIGH_QUALITY_CARE` for answers about pay and working conditions for caregivers, which the models code as `SOLUTION_CAREGIVER_WAGES` or `SOLUTION_CAREGIVER_WORKFORCE_DEV`. Version 6 adds `NEED_CAREGIVER_JOB_QUALITY`, which may be the code for these answers. Where Bree uses `NEED_OTHER`, the models usually find a specific code, such as `NEED_DIRECT_FINANCIAL_ASSISTANCE` for an answer that reads “Money.” - **Most codes the models add come from domains Bree did not use on that answer.** Of the 95 codes Sonnet chose that Bree did not, 70 are in such a domain, mostly Solutions and Challenges (Opus: 84 of 109). The models code what has been hard and what would fix it alongside the support the person asks for. This is the open question of what gets coded. - **The two models agree with each other much more than either agrees with Bree**, and Opus agrees with Bree no more than Sonnet does. The differences point to the instructions and the codebook more than to the choice of model. Next steps: - Bree decides whether an answer is coded for everything it mentions or only for what responds to the question. If the latter, the coding prompt changes to match, and rerunning both models on these answers costs under a dollar. - Bree settles the boundary between Desired Supports and Solutions codes that describe the same thing, and when `NEED_OTHER` applies. - The next round samples answers within each question instead of whole files, so the survey questions with the most answers are covered. This round has 7 survey answers. - The interviews are added once Bree codes them. A second person coding the same answers would show how far two people agree, which is the standard the models should be held to. ## Every answer side by side Codes a model shares with Bree are in bold. [Type in the search box to find an answer or a code.]{.web-only} ::: {.cell .column-page} ```{.r .cell-code} # one code per line, bold where it is in `reference`; long code names wrap # only at underscores show_codes <- function(sets, reference = NULL) { map2_chr(sets, reference %||% map(sets, \(s) character()), \(s, r) { if (length(s) == 0) return("(none)") s <- str_replace_all(s, "_", "_") shared <- str_remove_all(s, "") %in% r if_else(shared, str_c("", s, ""), s) |> str_c(collapse = "
") }) } scope |> transmute( Question = question_label(question), Answer = text, Bree = show_codes(code_sets$Bree), Sonnet = show_codes(code_sets$Sonnet, code_sets$Bree), Opus = show_codes(code_sets$Opus, code_sets$Bree) ) |> tbl( page_size = 10, searchable = TRUE, columns = list( Question = colDef(minWidth = 80), Answer = colDef(minWidth = 240), Bree = colDef(html = TRUE, minWidth = 170), Sonnet = colDef(html = TRUE, minWidth = 170), Opus = colDef(html = TRUE, minWidth = 170) ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: :::
